options.content: changing raw materials or parts into finished goods
options.rationale: Correct: this is the meaning of manufacturing.
This is agriculture, a primary industry.

options.content: selling finished goods to customers in shops and markets
options.rationale: This is retail, a tertiary industry.

options.content: digging minerals out of the ground
options.rationale: This is mining, a primary industry.

explanation: Manufacturing turns raw materials or parts into finished goods; it is secondary industry.

stem: Putting ready-made parts together to make a bus is an example of which process?

options.rationale: Correct: parts are put together.
Processing changes the form of raw materials.
Packaging wraps and labels finished goods.
Mining extracts minerals.

explanation: Assembling combines ready-made parts into a finished product.

stem: A bakery makes 200 loaves, then changes its machines to make 100 buns. Which production method is this?

options.rationale: Correct: a set number of one item, then another.
Mass production makes one item continuously in huge numbers.
Job production makes one unique item to order.
The bakery uses machines and makes many identical items.

explanation: Batch production makes a set quantity of one product before switching to another.

options.rationale: This is farming.

options.content: protecting goods and giving information such as the expiry date
options.rationale: Correct: packaging protects and informs.
This is processing.

options.content: repairing and servicing the machines on the factory production line
options.rationale: This is maintenance.

explanation: Packaging protects goods, keeps food clean, carries information and helps sell the product.

stem: Nokuthula orders a metal gate made to fit her yard exactly. Which production method will the welder use?

options.rationale: Mass production makes identical items in huge numbers.
Batch production makes sets of identical items.
Correct: one unique item to the customer's order.
An assembly line produces many identical items.

explanation: Job production makes a single item to a customer's specification.
hints: How many gates of this exact size will be made?

stem: Why does mass production usually make goods **cheaper**?

options.content: Workers in factories are never paid
options.rationale: Factory workers are paid wages.

options.content: The cost per item falls when huge numbers are made
options.rationale: Correct: fixed costs are spread over many items.

options.content: Machines need no electricity or maintenance
options.rationale: Machines do need power and maintenance.

options.content: Raw materials are given free to factories
options.rationale: Factories buy their raw materials.

explanation: Producing large quantities spreads the cost of machines and buildings over many items, lowering the cost of each one.

stem: A soap factory replaces twenty workers with one new packing machine. Which is the **most likely** disadvantage?

options.content: The soap becomes impossible to sell
options.rationale: The product does not change.
Machines usually increase speed.
Correct: mechanisation can reduce the number of workers needed.

options.content: The factory no longer needs electricity
options.rationale: A machine needs more power, not less.

explanation: Mechanisation raises output but can reduce employment.
hints: What happens to the twenty workers?

stem: Which argument **best** supports adding value by manufacturing in Zimbabwe instead of exporting raw cotton?

options.content: It means cotton no longer has to be grown
options.rationale: Manufacturing still needs raw cotton.

options.content: It removes the need for packaging
options.rationale: Finished goods still need packaging.

options.content: It guarantees that power cuts will end
options.rationale: Manufacturing does not solve power cuts.

options.content: It creates jobs and earns more from each bale
options.rationale: Correct: processed goods are worth more than raw materials.

explanation: Turning cotton into cloth and clothing adds value, creating jobs and higher earnings.
hints: Which is worth more: lint or a finished shirt?

stem: Processing, assembling and packaging are processes of manufacturing.
explanation: True. Most manufactured goods pass through these three processes.

stem: In mass production, each item is made by one person from start to finish.
explanation: False. Mass production uses division of labour: each worker or machine does one task on an assembly line.

stem: Match each example with the production method.

left.content: a carver making one stone sculpture by hand
a tailor sewing one wedding dress to order
a bakery making 200 loaves then 100 buns
a factory bottling drinks non-stop on a line

explanation: Each method suits a different scale and type of product.

stem: What name is given to making goods mainly by hand, with simple tools, in small quantities?
explanation: Handicraft production uses hand skills and simple tools.

points.description: Any one of: large quantities produced quickly; lower cost per item / cheaper goods; standard quality; workers specialise; goods can be exported; related jobs created
A second different advantage
A third different advantage

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Large quantities are produced quickly, goods are cheaper, and every item is of the same quality.

stem: Explain **two** disadvantages of modern methods of manufacturing.

points.description: Identifies: job losses as machines replace workers
Develops: families lose incomes and unemployment rises
Identifies: dependence on electricity / high cost of machines / pollution / boring repetitive work / loss of craft skills
Develops: e.g. power cuts stop the whole production line, so output and income are lost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Machines can replace workers, so some people lose their jobs and their families lose incomes. Modern factories also depend on electricity, so when there are power cuts the whole production line stops and output and earnings are lost.

explanation: One mark for each disadvantage and one for its development.
hints: Think about workers and about power.

stem: A small furniture maker in Gweru wants to produce more chairs without losing quality. Suggest **two** changes and explain each.

points.description: Suggests buying or sharing simple machines (e.g. power saw, planer)
Explains that machines speed up cutting and make parts uniform
Suggests batch production / dividing tasks among workers (cutting, joining, finishing)
Explains that workers specialise and become faster and more skilled, keeping quality high

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The furniture maker could buy or share simple machines such as a power saw and planer, so parts are cut faster and to the same size. He could also make chairs in batches and divide the work, with one worker cutting, another joining and another finishing, so each becomes skilled and quick at one task while quality stays high.

explanation: One mark for each suggestion and one for its explanation.
hints: Think about machines and about division of labour.

stem:
**Source A** — a description of a fictional peanut-butter factory in Marondera, 2026 (invented for this question)

> Groundnuts from local farmers are cleaned, roasted and ground by machines. The peanut butter is pumped into jars, which are sealed and labelled with the ingredients, weight and expiry date. Each worker has one job: some roast, some operate the grinders, others check the jars. The factory produces thousands of identical jars a week.

Read Source A and answer the questions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which production method does the factory use?

options.rationale: Job production makes single items to order.
The factory uses machines.
The factory produces for sale, not for its own use.
Correct: thousands of identical jars made by machines and specialised workers.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify **one** example of processing and **one** example of packaging from the source.

points.description: Processing: cleaning, roasting or grinding the groundnuts
Packaging: filling, sealing or labelling the jars

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Processing: roasting and grinding the groundnuts. Packaging: sealing and labelling the jars.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how the factory benefits local farmers and the community.

points.description: It buys groundnuts from local farmers, giving them a market and income
It employs workers (roasting, grinding, checking), giving jobs
It adds value to a local crop / supplies a local product, reducing imports

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The factory buys groundnuts from local farmers, giving them a reliable market and income. It employs local people to roast, grind and check the product. It also adds value to a local crop, so peanut butter does not have to be imported.

explanation: A source-based practice item on manufacturing processes and methods.
hints: In (c), think about farmers, workers and the country.

stem: This question is about modern manufacturing.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the difference between handicraft production and mass production.

points.description: Handicraft: goods made by hand with simple tools
in small quantities, each item often unique (e.g. a carved stool)
Mass production: goods made by machines on an assembly line
in huge numbers of identical items with division of labour (e.g. bottled drinks)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Handicraft production makes goods by hand with simple tools, in small quantities, and each item is often unique, like a carved stool. Mass production uses machines on an assembly line, with each worker doing one task, to make huge numbers of identical items such as bottled drinks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Modern methods of manufacturing have done more good than harm in Zimbabwe." How far do you agree?

points.description: Good: large output of cheaper, standard goods; value added to local raw materials; exports
Good: jobs in factories and related services; skills and technology
Harm: machines replace workers; costly machines and dependence on power; pollution; loss of craft skills
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Modern methods have brought clear benefits. Factories produce large quantities of cheaper, standard goods such as mealie-meal, cooking oil and clothing. They add value to local raw materials like maize, cotton and groundnuts, and some goods are exported. Factories create jobs, both inside and in transport, sales and maintenance, and workers learn new skills.

There are also harms. Machines can replace workers, so mechanisation may reduce employment. Machines are expensive and depend on electricity, so power cuts stop production. Factories can pollute air and water, and cheap factory goods can push out craft producers.

I largely agree. Modern manufacturing has done more good, as it supplies goods and jobs and adds value, but its harms must be managed through training, pollution control and support for small producers.

explanation: A practice evaluative item on the impact of modern manufacturing.
hints: In (b), consider consumers, workers and the environment.
